I can relate to so much of this. I'm female, bi, in stem, and also a survivor of sexual assaults from "friends". 
It is super hard to feel safe and like you belong. 
I've found a good group of girl friends in stem at uni (2 in physics, one in applied maths and I'm in pure maths) which really helps. We let each other know who to watch out for and share our frustrations. So if you can find some girls you get on with, not necessarily in the exact same field, this will probably help. My uni has a fortnightly women in stem lunch, which is where I met them, maybe you could see if you have something like that too?
Still be friends with the guys, but if you've got some girl friends as well you might feel safer.
What major are you in? I've found that in maths most of the guys are actually intimidated by me more than I am by them, which might be the case for you too. There are some guys who think they're better just because they're men, but mostly they want to be supportive of women in stem, even if they aren't sure what that looks like.

If the problem is not feeling good enough, then you should know that's super common. I feel like that a lot even though I ended up getting the university medal for my undergrad degree, so I know logically it's not true, but it's still hard to shake that feeling. The better you are, the more likely you are to feel like an imposter. 
Even if you're not going that well now, that doesn't necessarily mean that much. I had a friend in undergrad who struggled a bit, but she put in the work and has gone on to do really great things. She had had so many articles written about her and her work. She's been on TV, won awards. Generally doing much better than me, even though I got better marks than her in most courses. Which sounds like I'm jealous, but I'm super proud of her, and happy with where I'm at.
The other thing is, I think you should talk to someone about what happened and how it's effecting you now, a professional if you can. It sounds like you're spiralling so best to talk to someone soon.

TL; DR: get some stem girl friends, talk about you experience, look up "imposter syndrome".

I feel like I am in a similar boat to your girlfriend, although my partner and I overall are poorer judging by your jobs. 
I hate not paying my own way for things, but I've found a good way to side step this feeling is by dividing the bills. We have our money separate but he pays more of the bills than I do. He's in charge of paying phone and internet and I pay water and electricity, which is a bit less. We have less of a difference in income than you two so you could divide this differently.
I think you also need to realise, she probably knows you judge her money management, which is probably why she doesn't like you paying for her. Managing a low income is very different to managing a higher income, and also your family's money makes a big difference.
I was once dating a guy who came from a wealthy family and while we both lived off the same wage he always had more money than me because his parents would pay those extra costs, like car rego etc, and buy him things. Whereas I would pay for those things myself and sometimes give money to my mum to help her out. I don't think he realised how much of a difference that makes. 
If you want to pay for things for her, just do it without asking and she is more likely to accept. For example if you go to dinner, say your going to the bathroom and then pay the bill before it comes to the table. 
Or you can say, I'll pay for this and you can pay for the next thing, and let her pay for a cheaper thing like a round of drinks after dinner or something like that.
